newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to appeal ruling on line-item veto law.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to appeal ruling on line-item veto law.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Friday his administration would immediately appeal to the Supreme Court a judge's ruling striking down a law that strongly expanded presidential veto power.
"I was disappointed and I intend to appeal it," Clinton said one day after U.S. District Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson declared the historic line-item veto law unconstitutional.
"I think the line-item veto is very important in helping preserve the integrity of federal spending and I hope we can sustain it and we have to appeal it," the president reporters.
The law gave him and his successors the power to quash individual spending items within budget bills.
"We have to let the Supreme Court have their say on it," and decide if it violates the Constitution, he said.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton administration lawyers would take the rare step of asking the Supreme Court to expedite the case, hearing oral arguments by June and reaching a decision before the court recess in July.
It is up to the court whether to agree to that request.

Presidents of both parties had long coveted line-item veto power because it vastly expands their room for manoeuvre in budgetary matters and enables them to prune spending bills to their taste without vetoing an entire bill passed by Congress. Traditionally, all-or-nothing had been their only recourse.
The Republican-led Congress approved the new privilege in March 1996 and Clinton, a Democrat, was the first president to benefit -- although he had not yet used it.
But six dissenting members of Congress filed suit claiming the law violated the processes laid out by the Constitution for making or changing a law, and the judge agreed.

The law includes a provision that allows the losing side in a court challenge to go directly to the Supreme Court. Legal experts have long expected that the nine high court justices ultimately would have the final word on the law's constitutionality.

The line-item veto law, which expires in eight years unless extended, took effect in January. Although a Democrat stood to reap the initial benefit, the reform was a key element of the conservative "Contract with America" agenda of the Republican Congress.

But Judge Jackson said in a 36-page ruling that the law "hands off to the president authority over fundamental legislative choices" in conflict with the separation of powers sought by America's Founding Fathers, and spares Congress from making "vexing choices" over which programmes to cut."
The law empowers the president to sign a spending bill and cancel specific items within five days, including appropriations, tax breaks covering 100 or fewer people and new or expanded entitlements.

Congress still has final say. A line-item veto can be overridden by a two-thirds majority in each chamber, just as in the case of normal vetoes. Forty-three of the 50 state governors have line-item veto power over their legislatures.
